headline: State desk: Massachusetts sets drive-thru rules; Indiana MMJ bills
dek: Massachusetts regulators set what dispensaries must file and when to refuse sale at a drive-thru; in Indiana, senators from both parties draft medical bills.
key_points: Massachusetts' Cannabis Control Commission issued a bulletin on 25 November listing what stores must submit, including camera proof that every vehicle occupant can be identified, before opening a drive-thru.
Stores must refuse service if they cannot verify or count everyone in the car, if an occupant is under 21 and not a patient, or if a buyer shows signs of intoxication.
In Indiana, Democratic Sen. Fady Qaddoura is drafting a 2027 medical cannabis bill, joining Republican Sen. Mike Bohacek, MJBizDaily reported on 25 November.
Republicans still hold both Indiana chambers after Democrats gained 16 House and five Senate seats in November.
body: Two states moved in opposite stages of the cannabis cycle this week. Massachusetts, one of the most mature adult-use markets in the country, published the detailed rulebook for drive-thru sales a week after allowing them. Indiana, which still has no medical programme, now has lawmakers from both parties drafting medical cannabis bills for the 2027 session.

The Cannabis Control Commission's Investigations and Enforcement Department issued a bulletin on 25 November for adult-use and medical licensees that want to add a drive-thru to an existing store. It follows the commission's 17 November vote, which we reported on 22 November, deciding that its existing regulations already allow drive-thrus as long as stores meet the security rules.

The bulletin turns that vote into paperwork. Stores must apply through the commission's alternative security provision request form, copying their assigned investigator or compliance officer. The submission must include a floor plan showing every camera used to identify customers; an updated security plan, which must also be shared with law enforcement; evidence that the municipality knows about the plan and any local approvals needed; and camera stills or footage proving the system can clearly identify every occupant of a vehicle.

Stores must also file standard operating procedures covering identification checks that keep out anyone under 21 who is not a registered patient or caregiver, keeping product out of public view, and positive camera identification at every entrance, exit and point of sale. The plan must say how the store will capture and count occupants when a vehicle's layout blocks the cameras; the bulletin names third-row SUVs and minivans as examples.
## When a store must say no

The bulletin lists the cases in which a drive-thru must refuse a sale: when the store cannot verify the identification of every occupant, when any occupant will not show ID, when it cannot tell how many people are in the car, when an occupant is under 21 and not a patient or caregiver, or when cameras still cannot identify everyone despite the store's safeguards. Stores must also refuse when a sale would put the buyer or public at risk, including daily purchases above possession limits, signs of intoxication, or a patient exceeding their allotment.

Approval can come with conditions. The commission may require extra safeguards recommended by the local police chief, though the bulletin says the chief's opinion is not decisive. Other possible conditions include drive-thru-specific staff training, exterior signs with the rules, vaporizer warnings and education materials at the window, and sales records that separate drive-thru receipts. Every store must pass an inspection before opening the lane. Operating without approval can bring fines, suspension or revocation.
> Massachusetts allowed drive-thrus in a vote. The bulletin shows the real price of entry: a camera that can see into the third row.
## Indiana: medical bills from both sides

Indiana's medical cannabis debate has a new sponsor. Democratic state Sen. Fady Qaddoura of Indianapolis told WPTA he is drafting a 2027 bill to legalise medical cannabis, MJBizDaily reported on 25 November. His plan has three parts: access for veterans and patients with conditions such as cancer, seizures and chronic illness; action on cannabis-related criminal records; and sales through licensed sources overseen by state agencies, including the Indiana Department of Health.

He is not alone. Republican Sen. Mike Bohacek announced in May that he is drafting a 2027 bill on medical use, taxation and impairment standards that would not legalise adult use, according to MJBizDaily. A Change.org petition started on 8 November by an Indianapolis CBD shop owner had passed 21,000 signatures by 25 November, according to MJBizDaily, calling for medical and adult-use legalisation, expungement, business licensing and protections for hemp firms.

The arithmetic is tighter than the momentum. Democrats gained 16 House seats and five Senate seats in November, ending a 14-year Republican supermajority in the House, but Republicans still control both chambers, 54-46 in the House and 35-15 in the Senate, MJBizDaily said, citing the Indiana Capital Chronicle. Gov. Mike Braun said in May he hoped opposition would soften but did not endorse Bohacek's plan. MJBizDaily also noted that Indiana was among the states that challenged federal rescheduling at the DEA hearings.

Neighbouring states frame the pressure. Michigan, Ohio and Illinois all allow adult-use sales and Kentucky permits medical use, and Qaddoura said Indiana residents keep crossing state lines to buy. Meanwhile Indiana's hemp-derived THC sector faces the new federal hemp definition, which takes effect on 11 December and limits finished products to 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container.

In Massachusetts, watch for the first drive-thru approvals issued under the bulletin and whether any host town adds its own limits. In Indiana, watch for the text of the Qaddoura and Bohacek bills when the 2027 session opens in January, and whether Republican leaders give either a committee hearing. The federal hemp change on 11 December will hit Indiana's hemp retailers first.
